newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil doubles mark bond, boosts risk profile.
newsitem.headline: Brazil doubles mark bond, boosts risk profile.

text.p: Brazil, elated and probably a bit startled by the huge success of its 500 million mark bond, doubled the issue Wednesday to seize ripe market conditions and boost its drive for a credit upgrade, market analysts said.

"The fundamental objective for the government is to diminish Brazil risk. It is looking for ways to prove that Brazil has a better risk than the credit agencies claim and this is one way to do that," said Dany Rappaport, chief economist for MCM Consultores in Brazil.

Both tranches of Brazil's 10-year 1.0 billion mark ($610 million) bond priced at 230 basis points over the equivalent German Bund, a surprising 30 b.p. tighter than Mexico's 12-year 1.5 billion mark issue that also priced this week.
Despite Mexico's better credit rating - BB by Standard & Poor's and Ba2 by Moody's versus Brazil's B-plus/B1 - investors bought up Brazilain paper at a higher price.
The pricier Brazilian issue, officials argue, means the market sees Brazil as a less risky credit than Mexico.
"We think that this fact should be noted by credit agencies..Investors think Brazil is a better risk," Central Bank International Affairs Director Gustavo Franco told Gazeta Mercantil.

Credit agencies have had positive outlooks on Brazil ratings for over a year. But they say an upgrade will not come until the government makes more progress in slashing its fiscal deficit and passing key economic reforms.
And despite Franco's confidence, market watchers said the Central Bank was probably startled by the enormous success of the first tranche on Tuesday.

"I think Gustavo Franco was really surprised. He probably thought market conditions were favorable so why not get things done right now and double the deal," said a trader at an international bank in Brazil that participated in the syndicate.
In addition to improving Brazil risk, this week's mark bond was also seen as part of an ongoing plan to set benchmarks and create yield curves in a number of currencies.
As far as a new Brazil jumbo dollar deal, which has already been rumored in the market, most Brazil watchers don't expect it in the first half of this year.
"Brazil sees itself as an improving credit-upgrade story so doing a global might not make sense until they actually get an upgrade," said a fixed-income analyst at an international bank in Brazil.

Of the major Latin American countries, Brazil is the most infrequent visitor to world capital markets, primarily because it has no immediate financing needs like Argentina and Mexico. Over the past two years Argentina has issued 41 separate debt deals and Mexico has issued 18, compared to just seven for Brazil.

Brazil also does not have to issue as much as its neighbors because its corporations, which accounted for the vast majority of the $18 billion in Eurobonds issued by Brazil last year, have little trouble tapping capital markets. ((--Sao Paulo newsroom, 5511-248-5414))
